name: Ken Olsen
why_selected: Pre-1995 hardware founder: left MIT Lincoln Laboratory to cofound Digital Equipment Corporation in 1957 and built the minicomputer business, so the row tests a long employment apprenticeship in front of the venture and a rev10 crossing in the late 1950s/early 1960s that predates any modern trade press. Membership: https://computerhistory.org/profile/ken-olsen/ ("1996 Fellow ... For his introduction of the minicomputer as cofounder Digital Equipment Corporation")

name: Steve Wozniak
why_selected: Household-name hardware founder taken because the list's year order put him next, not skipped for fame (docs/BIASES.md 24): an engineer at Hewlett-Packard who designed the Apple I, giving a short employment-to-venture gap and a very fast rev10 crossing in the late 1970s. Membership: https://computerhistory.org/profile/steve-wozniak/ ("1998 Fellow ... For co-founding Apple Computer and inventing the Apple I personal computer.")

name: Gene Amdahl
why_selected: Pre-1995 corporate-scientist-turned-founder: roughly two decades as an IBM computer architect (System/360) before leaving in 1970 to start his own IBM-compatible mainframe maker, Amdahl Corporation, so the row tests a very late first venture and a mid-1970s rev10 crossing on machines sold a handful at a time. Membership: https://computerhistory.org/profile/gene-myron-amdahl/ ("1998 Fellow ... For his fundamental work in computer architecture and design, project management, and leadership")

name: Konrad Zuse
why_selected: Earliest-era recruit in the sample and a German-language sourcing test: built the first program-controlled digital computers in Berlin from the late 1930s, then commercialised them through his own firm Zuse KG from 1949. Expect a bounded rather than pinned crossing, since a 1950s West German computer maker published no revenue. Membership: https://computerhistory.org/profile/konrad-zuse/ ("1999 Fellow ... For his invention of the first program-controlled, electromechanical, digital computer and the first high-level programming language, 'Plankalkul'")

name: Carver Mead
why_selected: Academic-founder hybrid: a Caltech professor who taught and codified VLSI design and then cofounded a string of chip companies (Silicon Compilers, Synaptics, Foveon), so the row stresses which venture counts as the hit entity when the person's primary employment never left the university. Membership: https://computerhistory.org/profile/carver-mead/ ("2002 Fellow ... For his contributions in pioneering the automation, methodology and teaching of integrated circuit design")
